messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: low frequency, mid load; Ip = 25 uA peak, f = 50 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 680 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: high frequency, small Cp, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 200 Hz, Cp = 17.5 nF, RL = 4700 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: low frequency, large Cp; Ip = 25 uA peak, f = 50 Hz, Cp = 32.5 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: high frequency, large Cp, heavy load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 200 Hz, Cp = 32.5 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: hot, heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 200 kOhm, temperature 85 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       2.04    2.09    83.1   0.518      6.14  ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S3        4.2    4.21    23.2  0.0865      3.75  ok       FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL    
S4       1.79    1.82    57.1   0.759      3.21  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S5       1.74    1.74    8.96       -      20.1  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S6       1.55    1.56    25.4       -        12  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a sensor node (RL) from a piezo transducer.
    *   Constraints:
        *   $V_{out\_min} \ge 1.8\text{V}$
        *   $V_{out\_max} \le 3.6\text{V}$
        *   $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{V}$ (ripple)
        *   $T_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$ (startup)
        *   $dV \le 0.02\text{V}$ (settled)
    *   Piezo characteristics:
        *   Current source $I_p \sin(2\pi ft)$ in parallel with $C_p$ and 20 M$\Omega$.
        *   Open-circuit voltage amplitude $V_{oc} \approx 3.2\text{V}$ (S1).
        *   Varying conditions S1-S6 (frequency, $C_p$, load $R_L$, temperature).
    *   Reference (FBR) failures:
        *   S3: $V_{out\_max}$ too high (4.2V) - needs clamping.
        *   S4, S5, S6: $V_{out\_min}$ too low - needs better efficiency/voltage boosting.
        *   S2: $V_{pp}$ too high - needs more capacitance or better filtering.

    *   Standard FBR (Full Bridge Rectifier) is inefficient because it doesn't address the capacitive nature of the piezo.
    *   SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor) is the gold standard for piezo harvesting. It uses an inductor and a switch to invert the voltage on $C_p$ at the extrema, significantly increasing the energy extracted per cycle.
    *   Simplified SSHI (or SECE - Synchronized Electric Charge Extraction) can also be used.

    *   **Topology 1: SSHI (Standard)**
        *   Full bridge rectifier to charge the storage capacitor.
        *   An inductor $L$ and a switch $S$ in parallel with the piezo to invert the voltage at the peaks.
        *   Wait, the basic SSHI is usually: Piezo $\to$ Bridge $\to$ Cap, and an inverter (L + switch) across the piezo.
        *   Alternatively, a half-bridge SSHI.

    *   **Topology 2: SECE (Synchronized Electric Charge Extraction)**
        *   Uses a switch to connect the piezo to an inductor, then a diode to the storage capacitor.
        *   Typically: Piezo $\to$ Switch $\to$ Inductor $\to$ Diode $\to$ Cap.
        *   This is very efficient at extracting charge.

    *   **Topology 3: FBR with Zener Clamp**
        *   Similar to the reference but with a DZ33 zener diode to keep $V_{out} \le 3.6\text{V}$ (to solve S3).
        *   However, this doesn't solve S4, S5, S6 (low voltage).

    *   Wait, the requirements are quite tight. Let's focus on a robust SSHI-like structure.
    *   A common implementation:
        Piezo (pzp, pzn).
        Bridge:
        D1: pzp -> out
        D2: pzn -> out
        D3: 0 -> pzp
        D4: 0 -> pzn
        (This is the bridge).
        Inverter (SSHI):
        L1: pzp -> n1
        S1: n1 -> pzn
        Ctrl: SYNC (edges="both", ton=pi*sqrt(L*Cp))
        Storage:
        C1: out -> 0

    *   Let's refine the SSHI:
        If we use a full bridge, the inverter must be across the piezo terminals (pzp and pzn) to flip the voltage.
        $V_{oc} = 3.2\text{V}$. With a bridge (DSCH, 0.25V drop $\times$ 2), $V_{out\_max} \approx 2.7\text{V}$.
        The Zener is needed for S3 ($R_L$ is huge, $V_{out}$ will climb).

    *   *Design 1: SSHI with Full Bridge + Zener*
        Components:
        D1: pzp, out (DSCH)
        D2: pzn, out (DSCH)
        D3: 0, pzp (DSCH)
        D4: 0, pzn (DSCH)
        L1: pzp, n1
        S1: n1, pzn (ctrl G1)
        G1: SYNC (edges="both", ton=...)
        C1: out, 0
        D5: 0, out (DZ33) - to clamp at 3.3V.

    *   *Design 2: SECE (Simplified)*
        SECE typically uses an inductor and a switch to "dump" the charge.
        Piezo $\to$ S1 $\to$ L1 $\to$ D1 $\to$ C1.
        S1 closes at peaks.
        Wait, SECE requires a specific timing and often a diode to prevent backflow.
        Let's try a simpler version:
        D1: pzp, n1 (DSCH)
        D2: pzn, n1 (DSCH)
        D3: 0, pzp (DSCH)
        D4: 0, pzn (DSCH)
        L1: n1, out
        C1: out, 0
        S1: n1, 0 (ctrl G1) - This isn't quite right.

    *   *Design 3: Parallel-SSHI (Half-Bridge)*
        If pzn is grounded? No, the piezo is between pzp and pzn.
        Let's use the SSHI full-bridge as it is the most robust.

    *   **Wait, check constraints again.**
        $V_{out\_max} \le 3.6\text{V}$.
        $V_{out\_min} \ge 1.8\text{V}$.
        $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{V}$.
        $T_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$.
        S3 has $R_L = 4.7\text{M}\Omega$, which will definitely push $V_{out}$ up.
        S5 has $R_L = 150\text{k}\Omega$, which will pull $V_{out}$ down.
        S6 has $R_L = 200\text{k}\Omega$ at 85°C.

    *   The Reference FBR had $V_{out\_max} = 4.21\text{V}$ for S3. A DZ33 zener (breaks at 3.3V) will perfectly cap it at $\approx 3.3\text{V}$, which is $< 3.6\text{V}$.
    *   The Reference FBR failed $V_{out\_min}$ for S4, S5, S6. This means we need more power extraction. SSHI increases power extraction.

    *   *Refining Design 1 (SSHI):*
        L1: pzp to n1
        S1: n1 to pzn
        G1: SYNC, edges="both", ton=30us (starting point), phase=0
        Bridge: D1(pzp, out), D2(pzn, out), D3(0, pzp), D4(0, pzn)
        Clamp: D5(0, out) DZ33
        Storage: C1(out, 0)

    *   Wait, I can use a slightly different inversion. If I put the inductor and switch across the piezo, I flip the voltage.
        Current flow: Piezo charges $C_p$. At the peak, S1 closes, $L$ and $C_p$ resonate, flipping the charge on $C_p$. Then the bridge pushes that charge to $C_{out}$.

    *   Let's consider a second approach: a "Synchronous Rectifier" (using switches instead of diodes in the bridge).
        S1, S2, S3, S4 as a bridge.
        But SYNC only allows 2 controllers and 4 switches.
        I could use 2 switches for the inverter and 2 for something else? No.
        Stick to the diode bridge + inverter switch.

    *   Let's try a "Half-Bridge SSHI" if possible, or a SECE.
        SECE:
        L1: n1, out
        D1: n1, 0 (Wait, the bridge is better).

    *   Let's refine the "SSHI" one more time.
        Components:
        1. D1: pzp, out (DSCH)
        2. D2: pzn, out (DSCH)
        3. D3: 0, pzp (DSCH)
        4. D4: 0, pzn (DSCH)
        5. L1: pzp, n1
        6. S1: n1, pzn (ctrl G1)
        7. G1: SYNC (edges="both", ton=30u, phase=0)
        8. D5: 0, out (DZ33)
        9. C1: out, 0
        Total: 9 components.

    *   What if $V_{out}$ is still too low for S5/S6?
        The SSHI inversion improves the voltage $V_{pzp}$ seen by the diodes.
        The optimal $t_{on}$ is $\pi \sqrt{L C_p}$.
        For $C_p = 25\text{nF}$ and $L = 10\text{mH}$, $t_{on} = \pi \sqrt{10^{-2} \cdot 25 \cdot 10^{-9}} \approx \pi \sqrt{2.5 \cdot 10^{-10}} \approx 3.14 \cdot 1.58 \cdot 10^{-5} \approx 50\text{us}$.
        The evolution strategy will optimize $L$ and $t_{on}$.

    *   Is there a more efficient topology?
        A "Buck-Boost" style? No, we only have SYNC controllers.
        A "Charge Pump" style?
        Let's look at "SECE" again.
        SECE consists of a switch and an inductor.
        1. S1: pzp, n1 (ctrl G1)
        2. L1: n1, out
        3. D1: out, n1 (Wait, no)
        Actually, SECE is: Piezo $\to$ Switch $\to$ Inductor $\to$ Diode $\to$ Cap.
        But the piezo is AC. So you'd need two of these.
        1. S1: pzp, n1 (ctrl G1)
        2. S2: pzn, n2 (ctrl G2)
        3. L1: n1, out
        4. L2: n2, out
        5. D1: out, n1 (Wait, that's wrong)
        Correct SECE:
        S1: pzp, n1 (ctrl G1)
        L1: n1, out
        D1: pzp, n1 (Wait...)
        Let's stick to SSHI. It's a known high-performance architecture.

    *   Another option: **FBR with a larger capacitor**.
        The reference used 2.2uF. S2 failed ripple. S4, S5, S6 failed $V_{min}$.
        Increasing $C_{out}$ helps ripple, but not $V_{min}$. $V_{min}$ is a power balance issue.
        SSHI is the correct way to increase power.

    *   **Wait, what about the $V_{out\_max}$ for S3?**
        The FBR got 4.21V. A DZ33 zener clamps at 3.3V.
        3.3V is $\le 3.6\text{V}$. OK.
        Is 3.3V enough for $V_{out\_min} \ge 1.8\text{V}$? Yes.

    *   *Refining Design 2: A "Boosted" version?*
        Maybe use a larger inductor for the SSHI? (The optimizer will handle the value).

    *   *Let's try a different SSHI variation: "Parallel-SSHI"*
        In some versions, the inverter is placed *after* the rectifier.
        Rectifier $\to$ $C_{intermediate}$ $\to$ Inverter $\to$ $C_{out}$.
        But the standard SSHI (inverter across the piezo) is usually more effective for voltage.

    *   *Let's try a third topology just in case: A modified bridge.*
        What if we use a "Half-Bridge" rectifier?
        The piezo is floating (pzp, pzn). To use a half-bridge, one side must be grounded.
        But the piezo model has 20M$\Omega$ leakage to 0.
        If we ground pzn:
        D1: pzp, out
        C1: out, 0
        L1: pzp, n1
        S1: n1, 0 (ctrl G1)
        This would only harvest half the cycles.

    *   *Comparing SSHI vs SECE again.*
        SECE (Synchronized Electric Charge Extraction):
        S1: pzp, n1 (ctrl G1, edges="pos")
        L1: n1, out
        D1: out, n1 (Wait, the diode should be from the inductor to the capacitor).
        Let's try:
        S1: pzp, n1 (ctrl G1, edges="pos")
        L1: n1, out
        D1: out, n1 (No, this is wrong).
        SECE:
        - S1: pzp, n1 (ctrl G1, edges="pos")
        - L1: n1, out
        - D1: out, n1 (Wait, I'm confusing myself).
        Actually, the simplest SECE:
        S1: pzp, n1 (ctrl G1, edges="pos")
        S2: pzn, n2 (ctrl G2, edges="neg")
        L1: n1, out
        L2: n2, out
        D1: out, n1 (Still wrong)
        Correct SECE:
        S1: pzp, n1 (ctrl G1, edges="pos")
        L1: n1, out
        D1: n1, out (Actually, you just need a diode to prevent the capacitor from discharging back into the piezo).
        But the SSHI is more standard.

    *   **Final Proposal Selection:**
        1.  **SSHI-Bridge**: Full bridge + Inductor/Switch inverter + Zener clamp. (Most likely to work).
        2.  **FBR-Zener**: Full bridge + Zener clamp. (Baseline, just fixing $V_{max}$).
        3.  **SSHI-HalfBridge**: Since the piezo has a 20M$\Omega$ path to 0, maybe a half-bridge is simpler? No, let's try a variation of SSHI without the zener but with a very large storage cap to see if it's enough, or maybe a different inductor placement.
        Actually, let's go with a "Dual-Inverter SSHI" if possible? No, 2 SYNCs max.
        Let's try a "Charge-Extraction" (SECE) style for Proposal 3.
        SECE:
        S1: pzp, n1 (ctrl G1, edges="pos")
        L1: n1, out
        S2: pzn, n2 (ctrl G2, edges="neg")
        L2: n2, out
        D1: out, n1 (No...)
        Wait: S1 closes $\to$ $C_p$ charges $L_1$. S1 opens $\to$ $L_1$ dumps charge into $C_{out}$ via a diode.
        S1: pzp, n1 (ctrl G1, edges="pos")
        L1: n1, n2
        D1: n2, out
        S2: pzn, n3 (ctrl G2, edges="neg")
        L2: n3, n4
        D2: n4, out
        This is SECE. It's very efficient.

    *   *Let's double check the SSHI (Proposal 1) again:*
        S1: n1, pzn (ctrl G1, edges="both")
        L1: pzp, n1
        Bridge: D1(pzp, out), D2(pzn, out), D3(0, pzp), D4(0, pzn)
        Zener: D5(0, out)
        Cap: C1(out, 0)
        This is the classic SSHI.

    *   *Let's refine Proposal 2 (FBR-Zener):*
        Just a full bridge, zener, and capacitor.

    *   *Let's refine Proposal 3 (SECE):*
        S1: pzp, n1 (ctrl G1, edges="pos")
        L1: n1, n2
        D1: n2, out
        S2: pzn, n3 (ctrl G2, edges="neg")
        L2: n3, n4
        D2: n4, out
        C1: out, 0
        D3: 0, out (Zener DZ33)

    *   *Wait, Proposal 3 (SECE) has a problem:*
        It requires the piezo to be charged up. $C_p$ is in parallel with the source.
        In SECE, the switch $S_1$ closes at the positive peak. This connects $C_p$ to $L_1$.
        The energy stored in $C_p$ is transferred to $L_1$.
        Then $S_1$ opens, and $L_1$ discharges through $D_1$ into $C_{out}$.
        This is correct.

    *   *Self-Correction on Proposal 1 (SSHI):*
        The bridge should be DSCH.
        $V_{out\_max}$ might be an issue if the SSHI is *too* efficient.
        The Zener DZ33 is essential.
